text:
The European Commission on July 30 approved a EUR 290 million ($338.61 million) Dutch state aid package to support sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). The two approved support schemes aim to boost SAF supply and demand.

The two support schemes aim to support projects that produce SAF at different stages of their development. The schemes will share a common budget, but one will provide investment aid for SAF production while the other will help cover the costs of preparatory work for SAF projects, including front-end engineering design (FEED) studies.

Projects that use hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA) technology will not be eligible for either scheme. Rather, the programs will exclusively support advanced non-HEFA SAF and synthetic aviation fuels (e-SAF).

Aid provided via the schemes will be in the form of direct grants payable upon the completion of project milestones. The Netherlands plans to implement up to five rounds of funding between 2027 and 2031.

title: Renewable Gasoline Works. But Is It Feasible in the Market? - ResourceWise
description:
Show Real Market Availability First, the partners want to demonstrate the availability of renewable gasoline in an actual retail fuel market.
Repsol says it is currently the only supplier offering 100% renewable gasoline at public filling stations in Spain.
A renewable gasoline market ultimately has to answer several difficult questions: Where will the feedstocks come from?
Scaling Supply Is the Next Test Any attempt to significantly expand renewable gasoline production immediately runs into the issue that confronts much of the renewable fuels industry: feedstock availability.
The future of renewable gasoline depends not only on technical demand from gasoline vehicles, but also on its ability to compete for supply within a much larger low-carbon fuels market.
text:
For much of the past decade, the future of road transport has increasingly been framed around one dominant transition: replacing internal combustion engines with electric vehicles.

But there is another question worth asking. What happens to the millions of gasoline-powered vehicles that will remain on the road as that transition unfolds?

A new real-world trial in Spain could provide part of the answer.

In July, Repsol, Toyota Motor Europe, BMW Group, and Bosch launched a six-month pilot to demonstrate how existing vehicles can operate exclusively on 100% renewable gasoline under everyday driving conditions. The project will deploy a fleet of around twenty Toyota and BMW vehicles fueled with Repsol's Nexa 95 renewable gasoline. Bosch will provide digital technology to track and verify the renewable fuel used by the vehicles.

On the surface, the trial is straightforward. Put renewable gasoline into conventional vehicles and see how they perform.

But its implications go much further.

The pilot tests whether renewable gasoline can work across much of the existing transportation system:

Cars Using the Fuel

Filling Stations

Fuel Distribution Networks

Supporting Infrastructure Built Around Liquid Fuels

The pilot also tests whether the renewable origin and consumption of that fuel can be reliably tracked and certified. If those pieces work together, renewable gasoline could offer another route to reducing road-transport emissions without waiting for every existing combustion-engine vehicle to be replaced.

That is what makes this trial significant. It is also where the harder questions begin.

A Real-World Test of Renewable Gasoline

Repsol's Nexa 95 is produced from feedstocks compliant with the EU Renewable Energy Directive and is designed to be fully compatible with existing gasoline engines and infrastructure. According to Repsol, it can provide significant greenhouse gas emissions reductions compared with conventional fossil gasoline.

The pilot has three primary objectives.

1. Show Real Market Availability

First, the partners want to demonstrate the availability of renewable gasoline in an actual retail fuel market. Repsol says it is currently the only supplier offering 100% renewable gasoline at public filling stations in Spain.

2. Validate Refueling Data

Second, Bosch's Digital Fuel Twin technology will collect and validate refueling information using vehicle data, filling-station data, and fuel-card transactions. The goal is to create a transparent record showing that renewable fuel entered the market and was ultimately consumed by a particular vehicle.

3. Show Proof of Concept Under Normal Conditions

Third, Toyota and BMW vehicles will demonstrate that existing cars can operate on the fuel in normal conditions without requiring an entirely new vehicle or refueling ecosystem.

Taken together, those objectives make the project much more than an engine test. The partners are effectively testing a miniature renewable gasoline value chain:

Production and Supply → Retail Availability → Vehicle Compatibility → Fuel Consumption → Digital Certification

That distinction matters because the question of whether renewable gasoline works is no longer the only relevant one. The bigger question is whether it can work at scale.

The Existing Fleet Is a Decarbonization Challenge

Electrification remains central to the long-term decarbonization of passenger transport. But even rapid growth in electric vehicle sales does not immediately eliminate emissions from the existing vehicle fleet.

Cars can remain on the road for many years. Every gasoline vehicle sold today potentially represents years of future liquid-fuel demand. And the pace of fleet turnover differs considerably across countries and markets.

This creates a gap between changing the technology of new vehicles and reducing emissions from the vehicles already in use.

Renewable gasoline offers a potentially critical advantage in addressing that gap: compatibility.

Rather than requiring consumers to purchase a different vehicle or governments and businesses to first construct an entirely new refueling network, a drop-in renewable fuel could use existing engines, filling stations, storage tanks, and distribution infrastructure.

That does not make renewable gasoline a replacement for electrification. And it also does not mean that every gasoline vehicle could or should ultimately be supplied with renewable fuel.

It means the two pathways address somewhat different parts of the decarbonization problem.

Electrification can progressively change the composition of the vehicle fleet.

Renewable fuels could potentially reduce the carbon intensity of at least some of the liquid fuel consumed by the fleet during that transition.

Indeed, the European policy environment itself is evolving. The European Commission's December 2025 automotive package proposed maintaining a strong electrification signal while introducing additional technological flexibility.

Under the proposed framework, manufacturers would face a 90% reduction in tailpipe emissions from 2035. The remaining emissions would be addressed through measures such as e-fuels and biofuels.

The Repsol pilot therefore arrives as Europe is actively considering what a more technology-neutral approach to vehicle decarbonization could look like.

Technical Compatibility Is Only the Beginning

The appeal of renewable gasoline is fairly easy to understand. If a lower-carbon fuel can be introduced into an enormous installed base of vehicles and infrastructure, the challenges associated with replacing physical assets become considerably smaller.

But infrastructure compatibility should not be confused with market scalability.

A renewable gasoline market ultimately has to answer several difficult questions:

Where will the feedstocks come from?

How much renewable gasoline can realistically be produced?

What will it cost relative to conventional gasoline and competing low-carbon alternatives?

Where will producers earn the strongest returns for limited renewable feedstocks?

How will regulators determine and verify the emissions reductions associated with the fuel?

These are ultimately questions of markets, not engines. And they may prove far more difficult than demonstrating that a Toyota or BMW can run on renewable gasoline.

Scaling Supply Is the Next Test

Any attempt to significantly expand renewable gasoline production immediately runs into the issue that confronts much of the renewable fuels industry: feedstock availability.

Renewable fuel production depends on access to eligible renewable and waste-derived raw materials. Those resources are not unlimited, and renewable gasoline is far from the only market competing for them.

Renewable diesel, sustainable aviation fuel, marine fuels, and other low-carbon products are all drawing investment and policy support. Depending on production pathways and refinery configurations, producers must therefore consider two components:

Whether they can produce renewable gasoline

Whether gasoline represents the most attractive use of available feedstock and processing capacity

That competition becomes increasingly important as renewable fuel mandates expand.

A successful demonstration involving twenty vehicles will prove something useful about deployment. Scaling that proof of concept across thousands, and potentially millions, of vehicles presents a far greater supply challenge.

This is where the renewable gasoline story becomes an allocation story.

Limited feedstocks, production capacity, policy incentives, and demand from multiple transportation sectors will influence where renewable fuels ultimately go. If another market offers stronger regulatory incentives or higher margins, production may naturally flow there instead.

The future of renewable gasoline depends not only on technical demand from gasoline vehicles, but also on its ability to compete for supply within a much larger low-carbon fuels market.

Economics Will Determine What Technical Feasibility Cannot

There is also the unavoidable question of price.

Drop-in compatibility reduces one type of cost because consumers and fuel suppliers may not need to replace vehicles or build entirely new infrastructure. But the fuel itself still needs to compete economically.

Renewable feedstocks can command substantial premiums over fossil-based raw materials. Processing, certification, logistics, and compliance requirements add additional costs.

That means the commercial case for renewable gasoline will depend heavily on policy.

Several incentives can also influence the relative economics of renewable and fossil fuels:

Carbon Prices

Renewable Fuel Mandates

Tax Treatment

Emissions Standards

Credits

Without sufficient regulatory value for carbon reduction, the fact that renewable gasoline can be used in an existing car may not be enough to create widespread demand.

The market needs something more complicated than a compatible fuel. It needs an economic mechanism that assigns value to the emissions reduction associated with that molecule.

Proving the Carbon Reduction Footprint

That helps explain why Bosch's role in the Spanish pilot deserves particular attention.

The Digital Fuel Twin is designed to track renewable fuel through the value chain and verify its use in individual vehicles. At first glance, digital fuel tracking may seem secondary to the more eye-catching prospect of cars running on 100% renewable gasoline. In reality, it could be one of the most important parts of the project.

Low-carbon fuel markets depend on the ability to demonstrate that a product qualifies under applicable regulations and delivers a specific emissions benefit. As renewable fuels move through conventional storage, distribution, and retail infrastructure, credible chain-of-custody systems become essential.

Without reliable certification, an emissions reduction is difficult to translate into regulatory or commercial value. The challenge, then, is not merely moving renewable fuels. It is moving information alongside those fuels:

Where the fuel came from

What the fuel was produced from

How the fuel moved through the supply chain

Where the fuel was consumed

What emissions reduction can legitimately be attributed to the fuel

That means the infrastructure supporting renewable gasoline may ultimately consist of two overlapping systems: the physical infrastructure that transports the fuel and the digital infrastructure that verifies its environmental attributes.

From Twenty Cars to a Market

The Repsol, Toyota, BMW, and Bosch pilot will not answer every question surrounding renewable gasoline, nor should it.

Twenty vehicles operating for six months cannot demonstrate the economics of supplying an entire national vehicle fleet. It cannot create additional feedstock supply or determine how renewable molecules should be allocated among road transport, aviation, shipping, and other competing markets.

What it can do is test an important premise:

Can renewable gasoline move beyond controlled demonstrations and operate within today's transportation system?

If the answer is yes, the conversation changes.

The question is no longer whether renewable gasoline is technically possible. It is where it makes economic and environmental sense to deploy it, and how large that opportunity can realistically become.

That is a much more difficult and consequential consideration.

The transition away from fossil fuels will not happen simply by replacing one technology with another overnight. Vehicle fleets turn over gradually. Infrastructure takes time to build. Feedstocks are constrained. Regulations evolve. Consumers respond to price, convenience, and availability.

Renewable gasoline's most compelling proposition may be less about competing with electric vehicles and more about addressing a problem electrification cannot solve immediately. We must reduce emissions from combustion-engine vehicles that are already on the road.

The Spanish pilot suggests that the fuel, vehicles, filling stations, and digital tools can potentially work together. Now comes the hard part: determining whether the feedstocks, economics, policy frameworks, and supply chains can do the same.

What's Next for the Biofuels Market?

Renewable gasoline is only one part of a much larger and increasingly interconnected biofuels market. Competition for feedstocks, changing regulations, international trade flows, and growing demand from road transport, aviation, and marine markets will influence where renewable fuels are produced, how they are priced, and where they ultimately find markets.

ResourceWise will explore these dynamics in our upcoming Biofuels Market Outlook: Q4 2026 webinar.

The webinar will examine where biofuel markets are heading following Q3:

Where feedstocks are tightening or becoming oversupplied

Developments around 45Z and US policy

RED III and European market dynamics

Chinese HVO exports

Emerging advanced feedstocks

The latest developments in sustainable aviation and marine biofuels

title: Indepth: Operation Blue Skies AI contrail trial | International Airport Review
authors: Gabriel Higgins, Denise Pronk, Sara Solis, Leonardo S.p.A, Smiths Detection, Holly Miles, Louie Orbeta, Patrick Cuschieri, Trevor Strome, Solidarity Transport Hub Poland
description:
Operation Blue Skies has launched as the world’s first state-backed trial to use artificial intelligence to reduce warming contrails across an entire oceanic airspace, marking a major step towards lowering aviation’s climate impact through coordinated operational changes.
The 30-month programme will focus on the eastern half of the North Atlantic’s Shanwick airspace, which accounts for around 5% of global contrail warming.
NATS said Shanwick was selected because atmospheric modelling shows not only that it accounts for around 5% of global contrail warming, but also that a significant proportion of that warming occurs during the winter months between November and February.
The trial also reflects the operational complexity of managing one of the world’s busiest oceanic flight corridors.
Operation Blue Skies brings together Google UK, NATS, Contrails.org, Imperial College London, the University of Cambridge and the Met Office.
text:
Operation Blue Skies has launched as the world’s first state-backed trial to use artificial intelligence to reduce warming contrails across an entire oceanic airspace, marking a major step towards lowering aviation’s climate impact through coordinated operational changes.

The 30-month programme will focus on the eastern half of the North Atlantic’s Shanwick airspace, which accounts for around 5% of global contrail warming. Unlike previous initiatives involving individual airlines, the programme will test coordinated contrail avoidance across one of the world’s busiest long-haul flight corridors, creating what partners describe as the first large-scale operational blueprint for managing contrail formation across an entire section of controlled airspace.

Contrails, the thin cloud formations created when water vapour condenses around soot particles in aircraft exhaust, are estimated to account for roughly one third of aviation’s overall climate impact. Rather than relying on significant rerouting, Operation Blue Skies will use AI-powered forecasts to identify contrail-sensitive regions and recommend minor altitude adjustments, typically around 2,000 feet above or below an aircraft’s planned flight level, while remaining within standard flight operations.

NATS said the adjustments will be delivered through established air traffic control communication channels, allowing controllers to manage participating flights using existing operational procedures rather than introducing new systems. The organisation added that testing will be scheduled during periods of lower air traffic, helping minimise disruption while allowing controllers to evaluate how the approach performs in a live operational environment.

Two operational trials, each lasting around four months, will take place during the programme. Around 10,000 flights originating from hundreds of cities are expected to pass through Shanwick airspace during trial hours each year, with only a small percentage of flights requiring altitude adjustments to avoid conditions where strongly warming contrails are most likely to form.

Earlier airline trials paved the way

The programme builds on several years of operational research into contrail mitigation, demonstrating that today’s announcement represents the next phase of an evolving industry effort rather than an entirely new concept.

In 2025, TUIfly worked with the German Aerospace Centre (DLR) as part of the EU-funded A4Climate programme, with research aircraft following commercial flights through contrail-prone airspace to study how modern engines and operational changes affect contrail formation.

TUIfly also confirmed that it had rerouted several hundred flights during 2025 to avoid contrail-forming conditions, demonstrating that targeted operational changes could be incorporated into everyday airline services. The A4Climate programme also involved organisations including EUROCONTROL, FlightKeys, Imperial College London and other research institutions, helping establish practical approaches to climate-optimised flight routing.

Google’s earlier collaborations with American Airlines, EUROCONTROL’s Maastricht Upper Area Control Centre and FlightKeys similarly demonstrated that AI-generated contrail forecasts could be integrated into operational decision-making for pilots and air traffic controllers, paving the way for the larger-scale Shanwick trial.

NATS said Shanwick was selected because atmospheric modelling shows not only that it accounts for around 5% of global contrail warming, but also that a significant proportion of that warming occurs during the winter months between November and February. By concentrating the two operational trials during this period, the programme aims to maximise the climate benefit of each intervention by targeting the highest-impact weather conditions.

The trial also reflects the operational complexity of managing one of the world’s busiest oceanic flight corridors. While NATS will provide air traffic control services throughout the trial, AirNav Ireland will continue handling voice communications across Shanwick’s oceanic airspace, ensuring existing responsibilities remain in place as the programme is integrated into normal operations.

Operation Blue Skies brings together Google UK, NATS, Contrails.org, Imperial College London, the University of Cambridge and the Met Office. The programme is co-funded by industry partners and the UK Government through the Aerospace Technology Institute programme, while Google UK is contributing £1.4 million in AI research, engineering expertise and computing infrastructure on a pro bono basis.

If successful, Operation Blue Skies could provide a practical blueprint for expanding coordinated contrail mitigation to other busy international airspace corridors, demonstrating how AI, operational planning and collaboration between airlines, air navigation service providers and technology companies can reduce aviation’s climate impact while maintaining safe and efficient flight operations.

title: Google and the UK will steer planes around contrails over the Atlantic - TNW
description:
The UK government and Google are launching a trial to steer aircraft around climate-warming contrails.
Google and the project partners put contrail warming at roughly a third of aviation’s total climate impact.
That zone accounts for about 5 percent of global contrail warming, most of it in winter.
Google UK builds and verifies the models.
A verified cut in contrail warming across the airspace, confirmed by the Cambridge and Imperial teams rather than the operator.
text:
The UK government and Google are launching a trial to steer aircraft around climate-warming contrails. Google announced Operation Blue Skies on Tuesday. It is the first such effort across an entire ocean airspace. AI forecasts will predict where contrails form over the North Atlantic, and controllers will nudge planes to avoid those patches of sky.

Contrails are the thin white lines behind aircraft. They form when water vapour in jet exhaust freezes around soot particles into ice. Many vanish in minutes. In cold, humid air they persist, spread into cirrus cloud, and trap heat. Google and the project partners put contrail warming at roughly a third of aviation’s total climate impact.

Paul Hodgson, Google’s technical lead on the trial, gave the BBC a blunter version of the science. His five-year-old calls the lines “sky graffiti”, he told the broadcaster’s Tech Life programme. He added that the exact figure is uncertain. Scientists are confident it is “either quite a large problem or a very large problem”, he said.

What the trial actually does

Operation Blue Skies runs in Shanwick airspace, the eastern half of the North Atlantic corridor. That zone accounts for about 5 percent of global contrail warming, most of it in winter. The figure comes from the Aerospace Technology Institute, which is coordinating the public funding.

The intervention is small. Google builds AI forecasts from satellite imagery, flight data and Met Office weather models to predict where persistent contrails will form. Those forecasts go to NATS, the UK air traffic control provider. Its controllers can then tell pilots to change altitude by up to 2,000 feet, enough to miss the contrail-forming layer.

That manoeuvre is routine. Controllers already move aircraft to dodge turbulence and weather. The ATI said the deviations use standard air traffic control channels. New Scientist and the BBC reported that the trial focuses on evening and night flights. Those produce the strongest warming, because daytime contrails also reflect some sunlight back to space.

The numbers behind it

The programme is a £5mn, 30-month effort, the ATI said. The Department for Transport is putting in £2.65mn through the ATI Programme, and industry partners cover the rest. Google is taking part pro bono, contributing £1.4mn in kind through research, engineering time and computing.

There are two operational trials, each about four months. They run across the winters of 2026 to 2027 and 2027 to 2028, with roughly 20 to 40 test days per winter. Around 10,000 flights pass through Shanwick during trial hours each year. Only a fraction will be re-routed, enough to produce a statistically useful data set.

The consortium is a UK line-up. Google UK builds and verifies the models. NATS runs the airspace side and controller training. Contrails.org designs the trial parameters. Imperial College London and the University of Cambridge provide independent verification, and the Met Office supplies the forecasting. The ATI said all of the government grant goes to the academic, non-profit and aviation partners, not to Google.

Does avoiding a contrail actually help?

The obvious objection is fuel. Changing a plane’s altitude burns more of it, which emits more carbon dioxide, so the trial has to show the climate benefit outweighs the penalty.

The partners argue it does, and by a wide margin. A full deviation through Shanwick means about 100kg of extra fuel per aircraft, Hodgson told the briefing reported by New Scientist. He put the resulting carbon penalty at under 1 percent of the contrail warming avoided. He measured that warming “in the tonnes or even the tens of tonnes”.

The approach has a track record at smaller scale. Google has run earlier forecasts with American Airlines and others. The BBC reported those airline-level trials cut contrail formation or warming by around 60 to 70 percent. What is new here is that the instruction comes from the controller and covers every plane in the airspace, so airlines cannot opt out.

The awkward backdrop

The trial arrives as Google’s own climate footprint grows. The BBC noted that Google, like its rivals, is spending billions on power-hungry data centres to run AI, which environmentalists warn adds to the emissions the company is elsewhere trying to cut.

The desk has tracked that tension. Google’s $15bn India data centre ran into water and wildlife objections this month. The company has also promised $44bn of rent on data-centre buildings it will never own.

That buildout is the backdrop the BBC set the trial against. Google’s AI power demand is reshaping where it builds, and its data centres draw large and rising amounts of electricity. The company is cutting aviation emissions in one place while its own energy use climbs in another.

The UK government framed the trial as part of a broader push. Aviation minister Keir Mather called it “British ingenuity leading the way”, and pointed to £219mn already committed to sustainable aviation fuel. That sits alongside the government’s wider climate record, which this year included a UK solar generation record.

What would prove it works

Contrail avoidance is cheap next to rebuilding fleets or inventing new engines, which is what makes it attractive. It is also unproven at this scale, which is the entire point of the trial.

Three results would settle it.

A verified cut in contrail warming across the airspace, confirmed by the Cambridge and Imperial teams rather than the operator. Evidence that the fuel penalty stays as small as the partners claim once thousands of flights are involved. And a safety record clean enough that regulators would let controllers do this routinely.

title: SandboxAQ Makes AQCat Generally Available on Claude for High-Throughput Catalyst Screening
description:
AQCat lets any research team evaluate catalysts at a scale that once required specialized staff and hard-to-access computing power.
AQCat's accuracy comes from physics that other AI models leave out.
Anything that helps researchers reduce uncertainty is incredibly valuable, and SandboxAQ's MCP tools in Claude do that for both materials science and drug discovery."
AQCat is available today through Claude Science, on SandboxAQ's website, and AWS Marketplace.
About SandboxAQ SandboxAQ is a B2B company delivering solutions at the intersection of AI and quantum techniques.
text:
PALO ALTO, Calif., Aug. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- SandboxAQ today announced that AQCat is now generally available on Claude Science through Model Context Protocol (MCP), letting any researcher tap the company's Large Quantitative Model (LQM), an AI model trained to predict the physics of materials, simply by asking questions in plain English. AQCat identifies promising catalysts with accuracy approaching the field's most trusted methods, but up to 20,000 times faster, and it runs entirely through natural-language prompts with no coding required.

Catalysts are the hidden engine of the physical economy. They are the materials that speed up chemical reactions and make them practical at industrial scale, and they are essential to more than 80% of all manufactured goods and over 90% of all commercially produced chemicals, from fertilizer and fuel to fabric, glass, and plastics. Yet finding new and better ones has remained slow and expensive. Conventional lab methods typically test fewer than 100 candidate materials per week, a pace that keeps most progress limited to small, incremental gains.

AQCat lets any research team evaluate catalysts at a scale that once required specialized staff and hard-to-access computing power. It runs the first and most decisive step in the process: calculating adsorption energy, a measure of how strongly molecules stick to a catalyst's surface, which is the key early signal of whether a material will work. Teams can rank thousands of candidates up front and focus their modeling and lab budgets only on the most promising ones.

AQCat's accuracy comes from physics that other AI models leave out. Density Functional Theory (DFT), the long-standing gold standard for these calculations, is highly accurate but slow and costly, while faster machine-learning models often ignore magnetism altogether. AQCat is "spin-aware," meaning it accounts for magnetic behavior, bringing abundant, low-cost but magnetically complex metals like iron, cobalt, and nickel within practical reach. SandboxAQ trained it on AQCat25, a public dataset of 13.5 million high-fidelity DFT calculations spanning 47,000 intermediate-catalyst systems and every industrially relevant element.

"In catalysis research, a key bottleneck has been the number of surfaces you can realistically evaluate within compute and scientist resource constraints. Recovering DFT-quality adsorption energies at a faster speed changes the scale of questions my group can ask, and it opens up design spaces that were previously out of reach. Putting models behind a natural-language interface lowers the barrier for students and collaborators to participate in computational work," said Dr. Joe Gauthier, Assistant Professor of Chemical Engineering, Texas Tech University.

"Adsorption energy is the critical first calculation in most catalyst screening workflows, because it tells you how strongly a molecule binds to a surface and helps you prioritize what to study next. Many AI models overlook the magnetic physics that matter in earth-abundant industrial catalysts. We built AQCat to be spin-aware from the ground up, so it can recover near-DFT accuracy for magnetically complex systems, including iron, cobalt, and nickel, while running thousands of times faster than traditional approaches. Making it generally available on Claude means any researcher can run that calculation at scale, in plain language, without touching a line of code," said Aayush Singh, Head of Science, Catalysis, SandboxAQ.

The applications reach across green hydrogen, sustainable aviation fuel, fertilizer production, and plastics recycling, letting research teams pre-screen large design spaces before they commit DFT or experimental budgets and shortening innovation cycles that once took years.

Geoff Ling, Founding Director of the Biotech Office at DARPA, said, "In science, the biggest risk is often the unknown. Anything that helps researchers reduce uncertainty is incredibly valuable, and SandboxAQ's MCP tools in Claude do that for both materials science and drug discovery."

Executives note that sharing this proprietary tool allows the proven resource-recovery method to develop wider value beyond internal operations. Under this agreement, ZL Chemicals will market these solutions globally under the Vantis™ brand. The agreement utilizes Chevron’s technological expertise and ZL’s market capabilities to benefit operators in maximizing recovery and asset management.

Impact on the Chemicals and Materials Industry

This impacts the chemicals and materials industry by scaling field-proven surfactant formulas to improve shale and tight-reservoir oil recovery by up to 20% in new wells. It bridges the gap between operator-tied research and development and broad commercial availability through ZL's turnkey Vantis platform.

This business deal increases new well productivity and reduces decline rates in mature wells by making specialized chemical technology a globally available commercial service. It addresses industry limitations by offering a turnkey system for field execution and maximizing existing infrastructure rather than relying on new drilling.

The agreement breaks down siloed research and development by leveraging an external chemical partner to distribute advanced surfactant technology. Combining Chevron's lab-testing innovations with ZL Chemicals' global manufacturing enables a scalable solution for enhanced hydrocarbon recovery. This collaboration directly impacts the energy industry by extending the productive lifespan of mature assets through improved efficiency and overall well productivity for operators.

This technology further addresses key industry hurdles by clearing blockages in old wells to enhance oil flow without costly new drilling, extracting oil from tight shale rocks where recovery is normally low, and sharing proven field chemistry with independent operators rather than keeping it locked inside major oil companies.

Chevron's global innovation hubs, including the USD 1 billion ENGINE center in Bengaluru and the Ames Technology Center in Iowa, drive research, digital transformation, and technical excellence across worldwide energy operations. This National Aviation Day, the dream of flight is getting a whole lot greener.
text:
August 19 is National Aviation Day. President Franklin D. Roosevelt established the holiday back in 1939 to celebrate Orville Wright’s birthday. Wright, along with his brother Wilbur, built and flew the world’s first successful motor-powered airplane in 1903. That initial flight lasted just 12 seconds, but it completely changed how humans move around the planet.

More than a century later, aviation is facing another major shift. Engineers, pilots, and tech companies are redesigning aircraft from the ground up to make flying cleaner, quieter, and smarter.

Electric Airplanes and Air Taxis

Heavy batteries have made electric commercial flights tricky. But small electric aircraft are already taking off for short trips.

Companies are testing electric vertical takeoff and landing vehicles, often called eVTOLs or air taxis. They use multiple small rotors powered by electric motors to lift off like a helicopter and fly like a plane. Because they run on batteries, they produce zero direct carbon emissions and operate much quieter than traditional helicopters. Cities could soon use them to move people over heavy traffic without adding cars to the road.

Cleaner Jet Fuels

For big long-haul passenger jets, batteries are still too heavy. That’s why airlines are switching to sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF.

SAF is made from renewable sources like used cooking oil, agricultural waste, and household garbage. When mixed with standard jet fuel, it cuts carbon emissions by up to 80 percent across its lifecycle. Engine makers are testing planes that run on 100 percent SAF without needing any mechanical changes to the aircraft.

Hydrogen and Better Materials

Another path to cleaner flight is liquid hydrogen. When hydrogen burns in an engine or powers a fuel cell, the only byproduct is water vapor. Designing planes to hold bulky hydrogen tanks takes work, but major aviation firms are building test models right now.

At the same time, lighter materials like carbon fiber composites are replacing heavy metals in airplane bodies. Lighter planes use less fuel, no matter what powers them.

Autonomous Flying Systems

Modern commercial jets already use autopilot for most of the flight. Now, advanced flight software and AI sensors are making aircraft systems even smarter.

Cargo companies are experimenting with autonomous supply planes to deliver packages to remote towns where pilots might be hard to find. These systems use smart cameras and radar to monitor weather patterns and navigate safely in real time.

The Wright brothers used wood and canvas to build their first plane in a small bicycle shop. Today, aviation teams use lightweight composites, clean fuels, and electric motors. This National Aviation Day, the dream of flight is getting a whole lot greener.

Aviation remains one of the hardest sectors to decarbonize. Long-haul flights require high-energy-density fuels that current electric or hydrogen systems cannot consistently deliver at scale. The sector continues to depend on liquid fuels for operational reliability and global connectivity.

Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) has emerged as one of the most practical near-term solutions for reducing lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions. Why Sustainable Aviation Fuel Has Become a Strategic Priority

The aviation industry is under increasing pressure to align with global decarbonization targets while maintaining operational efficiency and growth. Unlike other sectors, aviation has limited alternatives to liquid fuels due to strict energy density, safety, and performance requirements. This constraint has positioned sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) as a central pillar in aviation’s decarbonization strategy.

Global frameworks are reinforcing this transition. The Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), introduced by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), requires airlines to offset growth in emissions from international flights. At the same time, several countries are introducing SAF blending mandates and long-term decarbonization roadmaps. These regulatory measures are shifting SAF from a voluntary initiative to a compliance-driven requirement.

Airlines are also setting independent net-zero targets, often aiming for carbon neutrality by 2050. Major carriers are entering long-term offtake agreements with SAF producers to secure future fuel supply. These agreements reflect a structural shift in fuel procurement strategies, where sustainability considerations are integrated into long-term planning rather than treated as a short-term adjustment.

Government incentives are accelerating this transition. Policy mechanisms such as the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS), federal tax credits, and production incentives are improving the commercial viability of SAF.

Rising demand for low-carbon aviation is further strengthening SAF adoption. Corporate travel policies, investor expectations, and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) frameworks are driving airlines to reduce their carbon footprint. SAF provides an immediate and scalable pathway to achieve measurable emissions reductions without requiring changes to aircraft fleets or airport infrastructure.

SAF is expected to remain the primary decarbonization pathway for long-haul aviation. Electric and hydrogen-powered aircraft are under development, but their commercial deployment at scale remains limited by technological and infrastructure constraints. In contrast, SAF can be blended with conventional jet fuel and used within existing systems, making it the most practical solution for near- to medium-term decarbonization.

As a result, SAF is transitioning from an alternative fuel option to a strategic necessity. Its role is expanding across regulatory compliance, corporate sustainability strategies, and long-term fuel security planning. This shift is driving increased investment, innovation, and collaboration across the aviation and energy sectors.

What is Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF)?

Sustainable aviation fuel is a renewable jet fuel produced from non-fossil feedstocks such as biomass, waste oils, and agricultural residues. It is chemically similar to conventional jet fuel and can be blended for use in existing aircraft, enabling lower lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions without infrastructure changes.

Why Biomass is Emerging as the Preferred SAF Feedstock

Biomass is gaining strategic importance as a feedstock for sustainable aviation fuel because it meets three critical requirements at scale: availability, compatibility, and sustainability. As SAF demand accelerates, stakeholders are prioritizing feedstocks that can support long-term production without creating supply constraints or infrastructure disruptions.

One of the primary advantages of biomass is its widespread availability. Agricultural residues, forestry waste, municipal solid waste, and animal waste are generated continuously across regions. The U.S. Department of Energy’s Billion-Ton assessments show that the United States has the potential to add over 400 million tons of biomass annually, bringing the total available biomass to more than 1 billion tons.

Biomass also benefits from existing supply chains. Collection and transportation systems are already established within agriculture, forestry, and waste management sectors. This reduces the need for new infrastructure and enables faster commercialization compared to alternative feedstocks that require dedicated systems.

Feedstock diversity further strengthens its position. Biomass includes a wide range of inputs, from residues to energy crops, allowing flexible sourcing based on regional availability. This reduces supply risk and supports consistent production across different geographies.

From a sustainability perspective, biomass aligns with circular economy principles. Many feedstocks are derived from waste streams that would otherwise contribute to emissions or landfill accumulation. Converting these materials into SAF improves resource efficiency and reduces lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions compared to conventional jet fuel. Biomass also supports energy security by enabling domestic fuel production. Countries can leverage local resources to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels and improve supply resilience.

Compared to other SAF feedstocks, biomass presents fewer scalability constraints. Waste oils face limited supply, while synthetic fuels require significant infrastructure development. Biomass, in contrast, is already available at scale and compatible with multiple conversion pathways, making it a practical option for near-term expansion.

As SAF demand continues to rise, securing reliable and scalable feedstocks will remain critical. Biomass meets these requirements effectively, positioning it as a preferred feedstock for sustainable aviation fuel production.

How Biomass is Converted into Sustainable Aviation Fuel

Biomass conversion into SAF involves multiple industrial pathways. Each pathway is designed to process specific feedstocks and produce fuel that meets aviation-grade specifications. The process is defined by three stages: feedstock preparation, conversion, and fuel upgrading.

The U.S. Department of Energy notes that approved SAF pathways can deliver significant lifecycle emissions reductions while remaining compatible with existing jet engines.

At a high level, biomass such as agricultural residues, forestry waste, and used oils is first processed into intermediate forms. These intermediates are then refined into hydrocarbons that closely match conventional jet fuel.

Conversion Pathways Table

How the Process Works Across Pathways

Each pathway differs in chemistry, but the core process remains consistent. Biomass is first collected and pre-treated to remove moisture and impurities. This step ensures stable conversion and improves efficiency.

In thermochemical routes such as gasification, biomass is exposed to high temperatures with limited oxygen. This produces synthesis gas, which is then converted into liquid hydrocarbons through catalytic processes. In biochemical pathways, biomass is fermented into alcohols before undergoing catalytic upgrading. The final stage focuses on refining and blending. The produced fuel is treated to meet aviation standards and blended with conventional jet fuel. Current approvals typically allow blending ratios of up to 50%, depending on the pathway.

According to the DOE Bioenergy Technologies Office, improving conversion efficiency and reducing processing costs remain critical for scaling these technologies.

Why Conversion Technology Matters

Conversion pathways directly influence cost, scalability, and emissions performance. HEFA remains the most commercially mature route due to established supply chains for waste oils. However, its scalability is limited by feedstock availability.

Thermochemical pathways such as Fischer-Tropsch offer higher scalability potential because they utilize abundant biomass residues. Similarly, Alcohol-to-Jet processes benefit from existing ethanol infrastructure, particularly in regions with strong biofuel ecosystems.

As technology advances, the industry is shifting toward pathways that balance feedstock flexibility, cost efficiency, and large-scale production potential. These factors will determine how quickly biomass-based SAF can move from pilot projects to mainstream aviation fuel supply.

Business Advantages of Biomass-Based SAF

Biomass-based SAF offers measurable operational and financial advantages. These benefits are driving adoption across airlines, fuel producers, and policymakers. The value extends beyond emissions reduction to supply security and regulatory alignment.

100% SAF can reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by up to 94% compared to conventional jet fuel, depending on feedstock and pathway. Other publications, such as those from Resources for the Future, highlight that scaling up biofuels production can strengthen rural economies and reduce dependence on imported fuels.

Despite strong momentum, scaling biomass-based SAF involves structural and economic challenges. These barriers are shaping investment decisions and deployment timelines. It also emphasizes the need to expand sustainable biomass supply without impacting food systems or the balance of land use.

Policy is Accelerating Biomass-Based SAF Development

Policy frameworks are shaping the commercial viability of biomass-based SAF. Governments are aligning climate targets with fuel transition strategies, creating a structured demand environment for SAF adoption. The focus has shifted from pilot support to market creation and long-term scale-up.

In the U.S., policy is designed to reduce cost barriers and accelerate private investment. The U.S. Department of the Treasury's IRS introduced a dedicated SAF tax credit ranging from USD 1.25 to USD 1.75 per gallon, depending on lifecycle emissions performance. This directly links financial incentives to improvements in carbon intensity, encouraging the use of low-emission biomass feedstocks.

In parallel, the U.S. Department of Energy is funding demonstration and commercialization projects to bridge the gap between pilot-scale technologies and industrial deployment.

How Policy is Structuring the SAF Market

Policy support is not limited to subsidies. It is creating a multi-layered ecosystem that reduces risk across the value chain. Federal and state programs are aligning feedstock production, fuel conversion, and airline adoption under a common framework.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture is supporting biomass supply chains through programs that fund feedstock cultivation, collection, and processing infrastructure. This ensures consistent availability of raw materials for SAF production.

On the demand side, federal agencies are integrating SAF into procurement strategies. Government-backed offtake agreements are improving revenue visibility for producers, which is critical for financing large-scale facilities.

Policy Impact on Investment and Scaling

Policy clarity is reducing uncertainty for investors. Long-term tax credits and funding programs are improving project bankability. This is leading to increased participation from energy companies, aviation stakeholders, and infrastructure developers.

At the same time, sustainability criteria embedded in policies are shaping feedstock selection. Incentives favor pathways that deliver greater emissions reductions, thereby accelerating the shift toward waste-based and residue-derived biomass.

Why Policy Support Matters for Biomass

Biomass-based SAF depends on coordinated development across agriculture, energy, and aviation sectors. Policy frameworks are enabling this integration by aligning incentives across all three domains.

As a result, biomass is moving from a supplementary feedstock to a policy-backed priority, supported by structured incentives, funding mechanisms, and long-term decarbonization mandates.

The Future of Biomass in Sustainable Aviation Fuel

Biomass is expected to remain central to SAF production over the next decade. Advanced feedstocks, including algae and engineered biomass, are expanding the resource base.

Bio-refineries are evolving into integrated production hubs. Carbon capture technologies such as BECCS are being integrated to further reduce lifecycle emissions. The International Energy Agency highlights that bioenergy with carbon capture can deliver negative emissions under certain conditions. AI-driven supply chain optimization is improving feedstock sourcing and logistics. These developments support long-term scalability and cost efficiency. Biomass is likely to remain a dominant SAF feedstock through 2035 due to its availability, policy support, and compatibility with existing fuel systems.

What This Means for Stakeholders Across the Value Chain

Biomass-based SAF is moving beyond early-stage momentum and entering a phase where execution determines impact. The direction is clear. The next phase depends on how effectively stakeholders align operations, investment, and supply chains.

For fuel producers, the focus is shifting toward process efficiency and feedstock flexibility. Technologies that can handle diverse biomass inputs will reduce supply risk and improve margins. For airlines, long-term procurement strategies will become central to managing both cost exposure and emissions targets.

What emerges is a clear industry shift. Biomass-based SAF is not defined only by environmental value. It is increasingly tied to energy diversification, supply resilience, and long-term cost stability. The companies that move early to secure feedstock, invest in scalable technologies, and align with policy frameworks will be better positioned as SAF demand accelerates. The opportunity is not limited to fuel production. It extends across logistics, agriculture, refining, and aviation operations.

In this transition, biomass is emerging as a strategic enabler of aviation decarbonization, supported by real assets, existing supply chains, and growing institutional backing.

Bottom Line

Biomass is evolving from a renewable energy source into a strategic industrial feedstock. Its role in sustainable aviation fuel production is expanding due to its scalability, availability, and compatibility with existing infrastructure.

SAF represents one of the most significant long-term growth opportunities for biomass utilization. Governments, airlines, and fuel producers are investing across the value chain to accelerate deployment.

Long-term success will depend on sustainable feedstock sourcing, continued technological advancement, and supportive policy frameworks.

What is Sustainable Aviation Fuel?

Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) is an alternative to conventional jet fuel produced from renewable or waste-based resources. It is designed to operate within existing aircraft engines and fueling infrastructure while delivering significantly lower lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions than fossil-derived aviation fuel.

Why is biomass used to produce SAF?

Biomass is widely used because it is renewable, widely available, and compatible with multiple fuel conversion technologies. It includes waste streams that would otherwise remain underutilized. The U.S. Department of Energy identifies biomass as a key pathway for producing low-carbon fuels due to its ability to reduce lifecycle emissions and support domestic energy supply.

Which biomass feedstocks are used for aviation fuel?

Common feedstocks include agricultural residues such as corn stover and wheat straw, forestry residues, used cooking oil, animal fats, and municipal solid waste. These feedstocks are preferred because they do not directly compete with the food supply and are available at scale across multiple regions.

How is biomass converted into jet fuel?

Biomass is converted into SAF through several established pathways. These include hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA), gasification followed by Fischer–Tropsch synthesis, and alcohol-to-jet conversion. Each pathway transforms raw biomass into a refined fuel that meets aviation-grade specifications.

Australian aerospace start-up Stralis will close after completing the first taxi of its hydrogen-electric aircraft at Brisbane International Airport, a feat it called the first in the Southern Hemisphere.

In a farewell statement, the firm said it had proven that hydrogen aviation technology works, but it was unable to bridge the gap to commercial feasibility in time to sustain operations.

The firm’s Beechcraft Bonanza A36 single-propeller light aircraft taxied, powered by a fuel cell system that Stralis claimed was set to provide 10 times greater range than battery-electric and run at 20-50% lower costs than fossil fuel-powered flight.

Calling the commercialisation of hydrogen-fuelled aircraft a “capital-intensive journey,” the firm repeated its belief that the molecule will play a part in future aviation.

It lamented that its commercial case “does not yet outweigh the additional costs, operational changes and infrastructure investment it requires.”

Stralis’ conclusion also spells the end for its early-stage drone hydrogen-propulsion technology.

Hydrogen in aviation has faced an uphill battle in recent years, with concerns about the fuel’s low energy efficiency, high-volume storage requirements and ground logistics of supply besetting innovators in the space.

In the near-term, airlines, governments, and aviation bodies remain focused on sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), with mandates and regulations spreading globally.

text: A big thank you to Australia and Japan for timing your sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) announcements around the Sustainable Aviation Futures webinar yesterday 👀 Two big items landed in the 24 hours prior, making for a fun and timely discussion. It was a pleasure to join Shubhodeep Pal, Melvyn Tan, Kenneth Lim, and Arnaud Brolly to talk through APAC supply and policy. So what's new from Japan and Australia? There's both retreat and growing ambition. 1 - Japan's 10% SAF target by 2030 was widely seen as a mandate. This has transformed into a 1% requirement at seven airports. It's a huge drop in ambition, and the policy instability doesn't give SAF investors confidence. 2- Australia launched the consultation on a demand side mechanism for Low Carbon Liquid Fuels. Across jet fuel, diesel, and petrol, they're proposing mandated volumes until 2035, before transitioning to a carbon intensity model. Blending is proposed at 1 to 4% by 2030. It's excellent to see Australia taking material steps on SAF policy. A few other takeaways from the discussion: 3 - The "why" for SAF is no longer just decarbonisation. There's increasing recognition of the value it brings to regional economic development, jobs, and in particular energy sovereignty. The Iran conflict has only pushed this conversation forward, highlighting the vulnerability of import-heavy supply chains and the role of local SAF production to help reduce it. 4 - APAC SAF targets are ubiquitous, but aren't necessarily legislated. This creates a gap between aspiration and action. As Kenneth pointed out, Thailand has had a 2026 SAF target (1%) in place for quite some time. It's Q3 2026, and there's still no movement. The news out of Japan reflects the same issue. More needs to be done to shift targets into concrete action that can help finance SAF facilities. 5 - The APAC region is diverse. The feedstocks, the ambition, the policy design. Melvyn highlighted the importance of regional cooperation to leverage local strengths and help manage fragmentation. Different rules in a closely connected region risks driving complexity, arbitrage, and unnecessary logistics costs. 6 - Brazil has just announced its regulatory Book and Claim scheme, and this is one to watch for Asia. As Arnaud noted, it will be a case of "wait and see" to understand how it works, and in particular how it interacts with the voluntary Scope 3 certificate (SAFc) market. Overall, there's a sense of optimism in Asia. With progress on everything from national roadmaps, to policy, to production facilities, there's serious momentum in this part of the world. Thanks to everyone who tuned in. The recording is in the comments and I'm always happy to discuss the SAF dynamics in APAC. And if you're looking at submitting on Australia's Low Carbon Liquid Fuel consultation (due 15 September), get in touch. Joulec will be submitting on the role of voluntary Scope 3 in policy design, and there's plenty else to dig into.

text:
EcoCeres has expanded its efforts to supply sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) in China through a new partnership that will see SF Airlines use the fuel for its outbound freighter flights from Ezhou Huahu International Airport in Hubei.

SAF producer EcoCeres has partnered with SF Group and China National Aviation Fuel Group (CNAF) to launch a customised SAF commercial fuelling programme, in collaboration with the Second Research Institute of the Civil Aviation Administration of China (CASRI).

Under the programme, SAF produced by EcoCeres will be blended by CNAF and supplied to outbound freighter flights operated by SF Airlines out of Ezhou.

This would enable up to a 90% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions compared to conventional jet fuel, said EcoCeres, though it did not confirm how many of the flights out of Ezhou would be fuelled by SAF compared to standard jet fuel.

This collaboration builds on EcoCeres’ previous SAF pilot programme in China with CASRI, CNAF, China Southern Airlines, Air China Cargo, Sichuan Airlines, and Huarong Chemical.

This programme saw SAF produced at EcoCeres’ Zhangjiagang facility blended by CNAF and used to fuel commercial flights at Chengdu Shuangliu International Airport.

The latest project also leverages AnchorTrace, a Scope 3 environmental attributes platform jointly developed by CNAF and CASRI, enabling full lifecycle tracking, registration, and retirement of SAF environmental attributes.

“This project demonstrates how SAF can pragmatically and efficiently connect renewable fuel producers, aviation fuel infrastructure providers, and cargo operators in a results-oriented way,” said James Tam, co-chairman of EcoCeres.

“By integrating SAF into existing aviation fuel systems, we are working together with our partners to build a replicable, scalable and verifiable pathway for lower‑emissions air cargo development in China.”

“The successful inaugural flight of this project marks SF Group’s enhanced end-to-end capability, from bulk SAF sourcing, blending and customized fueling to freighter utilization, alongside a strategic green capacity deployment,” added Li Sheng, chairman of SF Airlines.

“It also positions SF Airline as the first in China to integrate three unique advantages: a SAF-enabled hub airport, large-scale physical SAF fueling capability, and international SAF certification, making it a Scope 3 green aviation service provider.”

Building on this collaboration, EcoCeres aims to further leverage its SAF presence in Hong Kong and Mainland China, connecting regional feedstock supply, production, and demand across both passenger and cargo aviation sectors.

text:
Syzygy Plasmonics has signed a framework agreement with the International Finance Corporation (IFC), the private sector arm of the World Bank Group, to support a pipeline of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) projects across Latin America.

Under the agreement, IFC will provide technical and commercial advisory services as Syzygy advances individual projects. The framework also sets out a path for further collaboration as the Houston, Texas, U.S.A.-based company scales its SAF platform across the region.

The first project supported under the framework is NovaSAF-1, a planned commercial-scale SAF facility in Durazno, Uruguay. As the first commercial deployment of Syzygy’s technology, the project is expected to demonstrate a new route to sustainable aviation fuel using renewable electricity and biogas, and to serve as a model for potential future facilities across Latin America.

Unlike conventional industrial processes that rely on fossil-fuel heat, Syzygy’s technology uses renewable electricity to power light-driven reactors that convert biogas into sustainable aviation fuel. The company estimates the process can reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by up to 90% compared with conventional jet fuel.

The collaboration comes as airlines look for scalable, lower-carbon alternatives to conventional jet fuel. By combining its light-driven technology with Latin America’s renewable energy resources and biogas feedstocks, Syzygy aims to accelerate the commercialisation of SAF in emerging markets.

“The transition to lower-carbon aviation will depend on technologies that are not only innovative, but commercially viable and scalable,” said Raphaël Eskinazi, IFC regional investment manager for manufacturing and forests in Latin America and the Caribbean. “IFC’s role is to help bridge that transition: supporting pioneering projects that can mobilize private capital, demonstrate new business models and create pathways for broader market adoption across emerging economies.”

Trevor Best, co-founder and chief executive officer of Syzygy Plasmonics, said IFC’s involvement was a strong signal that the company is positioned to disrupt the market, citing its technology, project pipeline, and the commercial agreements underpinning them. IFC’s role in helping innovative technologies become commercially viable and replicable across emerging markets matches the ambition of the NovaSAF build-out, he said.

Commercial agreements already underpin the regional expansion. Trafigura has signed a binding offtake agreement covering the full production of NovaSAF-1, while Trafigura and World Fuel Services have entered capacity reservation agreements for future facilities across the region. Syzygy has also secured feedstock agreements with several partners, including Estancias del Lago and Geo bio gas&carbon. Together, the company said, the agreements support a long-term growth strategy targeting up to one million metric tonnes of annual SAF production capacity in Brazil by 2035.

Founded in 2017, Syzygy Plasmonics develops light-driven photocatalytic reactors for industrial chemical production. Its platform, based on technology licensed from Rice University, uses renewable electricity instead of fossil-fuel combustion to enable cleaner, lower-cost production of hydrogen, SAF, and other chemicals. The company’s NovaSAF portfolio of biogas-to-SAF facilities targets commercial-scale operations from 2028.

IFC noted that its expression of interest in financing is subject to project appraisal, board approval, and the satisfaction of its standard investment criteria and environmental and social standards. Individual project investments have not yet been approved.

text: Europe earmarks up to €1.6 billion of ETS allowances for the airlines ✈️ that use sustainable aviation fuel. The producers 🏭 that make it got €153 million in grants. Ten to one. A distributional fight waiting to happen — who should get the money, users or producers? My new essay argues this is the wrong question. Under ReFuelEU's binding blending shares, the mandate pins the quantity; a per-litre subsidy then moves money, not fuel — and whoever cashes the cheque, competition passes it through to airlines and their passengers. Placement doesn't matter. Form does. What builds plants is revenue a bank can price: contracts, auctions, capital grants. Guaranteed demand alone is not it — Britain runs a SAF mandate of its own and is bolting a revenue-certainty mechanism on top for exactly that reason. Tellingly, the airline industry itself now asks for producer support. The economics says the preference is rational: the fuel must exist and stay affordable, and the form that builds plants lives on the producer side. Neither per-litre money nor captive demand builds plants. Only contract design does. The full working — a bench experiment, Britain's contracts-for-difference evidence, America's cellulosic collapse and corn-ethanol lock-in, and what the Commission's proposed FEETS extension quietly changes — is in the essay 📄. text:
China is launching a commercial programme to use sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) in air cargo operations. The project brings together EcoCeres, logistics company SF Group and China National Aviation Fuel (CNAF), with the participation of a research institute under the Civil Aviation Administration of China.

Under the programme, EcoCeres will produce SAF, which will then be blended by CNAF and supplied to outbound cargo flights operated by SF Airlines. According to EcoCeres, the fuel can reduce greenhouse gas emissions by up to 90% compared with conventional jet fuel.

Ezhou Huahu International Airport in Hubei province, a major cargo hub for SF Airlines, will serve as one of the key locations for the programme. The companies see the project as a model that could eventually be scaled up for wider SAF use across China’s air cargo and logistics sectors.

The new programme follows EcoCeres’ previous SAF pilot project in China. During its initial phase, SAF produced at the company’s Zhangjiagang facility was blended by CNAF and used to fuel commercial flights at Chengdu Shuangliu International Airport.

Expanding SAF use creates an additional growth area for China’s biofuel market. In addition to aviation fuel, EcoCeres produces HVO and bio-naphtha at industrial scale, while further SAF development could eventually generate additional demand for biofuel feedstocks.

text:
The eFUEL GROUP and German lubricant specialist LIQUI MOLY have entered into a strategic partnership to further develop synthetic fuels and advanced lubrication technologies. The collaboration aims to optimize the interaction between eFuels, engine oils, and additives to improve efficiency, engine protection, and overall performance under real-world operating conditions.

The initial focus will be on motorsport applications, with plans to expand the partnership into additional mobility sectors in the future. Both companies see eFuels as an important component of a technology-neutral mobility strategy. According to the eFUEL GROUP, synthetic fuels can reduce new CO₂ emissions by up to 90 percent over their entire life cycle compared with conventional fossil fuels, depending on the feedstock and production pathway.

Another key advantage of eFuels is their compatibility with today's internal combustion engines and the existing refueling infrastructure. This makes them a practical solution for reducing the carbon footprint of the approximately 1.4 billion combustion-engine vehicles currently in operation worldwide.

As part of the cooperation, the partners will also investigate the interaction between fuels, engine oils, and additives. Modern low-viscosity lubricants help reduce friction losses, while specially formulated additives improve engine cleanliness and combustion efficiency. By optimizing these two "liquid components," the companies expect to achieve lower fuel consumption and higher overall drivetrain efficiency.

Through this partnership, the eFUEL GROUP and LIQUI MOLY are combining their expertise in synthetic fuels, lubricants, and additive technologies to accelerate the development of sustainable solutions for both existing and future internal combustion engines.

About eFUEL GROUP

The eFUEL GROUP develops projects focused on sustainable energy solutions, with activities spanning eFuels, Sustainable Aviation Fuel (eSAF), and Direct Air Capture (DAC). The company follows a technology-neutral approach, combining environmentally focused energy projects with attractive investment opportunities. A key objective is the reduction of new CO₂ emissions through synthetic fuels and innovative carbon capture and utilization technologies.

About LIQUI MOLY

Headquartered in Ulm, Germany, LIQUI MOLY is one of the world's leading manufacturers of motor oils, additives, and automotive chemicals. Founded in 1957, the company develops and manufactures its products exclusively in Germany and offers a portfolio of around 4,000 products, including engine and transmission oils, additives, greases, sprays, vehicle care products, adhesives, and sealants. LIQUI MOLY exports to approximately 150 countries and has been repeatedly recognized as one of Germany's leading lubricant brands.

METRO MANILA — The Department of Energy (DOE) - Philippines, in collaboration with the ASEAN Centre for Energy (ACE) and Leverage International, officially launched the 26th ASEAN Energy Business Forum (AEBF-26), setting the stage for a major regional gathering aimed at advancing energy cooperation, investment, and connectivity across Southeast Asia.

The forum is expected to bring together energy ministers from the 11 ASEAN Member States, global industry leaders, and more than 1,500 delegates from across the region and beyond.

AEBF 2026 will carry the theme “Clean Energy Unlocked: A Stronger ASEAN,” with the sub-theme “Driving Innovation and Investment Toward a Sustainable Energy Future.” The theme underscores ASEAN's efforts to accelerate clean energy development while deepening regional cooperation and economic integration, complementing the Philippines' ASEAN-26 Chairship theme, “Navigating Our Future, Together.”

Photo 2. The soft launch event officially commenced with a keynote address delivered by H.E. Sharon S. Garin, DOE Secretary.

Energy Secretary Sharon S. Garin said the Philippines' hosting of AEBF-26 provides an important opportunity to translate ASEAN's shared energy priorities into stronger partnerships, concrete investments, and projects that benefit the region.

“ASEAN’s energy future will depend on how effectively we turn our shared ambitions into concrete investments, stronger regional connections, and projects that deliver reliable, affordable, and cleaner energy to our people. As ASEAN Chair, the Philippines wants AEBF-26 to be a platform where governments, industry, and investors move beyond discussions and build the partnerships needed to unlock the region’s enormous energy potential,” Secretary Garin said.

ACE Executive Director Dato’ Ir. Ts. Razib Dawood underscored the scale of investment required to support ASEAN's growing energy requirements and clean energy transition.

“Our region needs around USD 200 billion in annual energy investment by 2030 and 75 percent of that, roughly USD 150 billion, must go toward clean energy. In 2021, we mobilized just USD 30 million. That gap is precisely what AEBF-26 exists to help close,” Dawood said.

Photo 3. Dato’ Ir. Ts. Razib Dawood, Executive Director of ACE, presented the AEBF-26 overview, followed by an address on “Connecting ASEAN Energy Priorities with Business and Investment Opportunities”.

AEBF-26 will feature policy dialogues, high-level roundtables, business-to-business engagements, and exhibitions covering key regional priorities, including the ASEAN Power Grid, Renewable Energy Certificates, energy efficiency, and energy financing and investment.

The Forum will also feature the Philippines Energy Investment Forum and the ASEAN Sustainable Aviation Fuel Conference, alongside the launch of the 9th ASEAN Energy Outlook and the ASEAN Energy Investment Report, as well as activities under the Sustainable ASEAN Energy Management Accreditation Scheme (SEAMAS) Program for the Energy Efficiency Certification Scheme.

Building on the previous AEBF held in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, AEBF-26 will provide a platform for governments and the private sector to advance regional energy priorities, develop partnerships, and help mobilize the capital and technologies required to meet ASEAN's growing energy needs.

The DOE and ACE are inviting stakeholders from government, industry, financial institutions, development organizations, and civil society to participate in AEBF-26 and contribute to discussions on ASEAN's energy future.

text:
Solarstic, a South Korean lightweight solar technology company, has raised pre-Series A funding from Stonebridge Ventures and IBK(Industrial Bank of Korea).

The investment will support the certification and launch of the company’s building-attached photovoltaics (BAPV) products and establish manufacturing infrastructure for vehicle-integrated photovoltaics (VIPV) components.

Founded as a corporate venture within Hyundai Motor Group, Solarstic has developed lightweight packaging and forming technology originally designed for vehicle-integrated solar applications and is now expanding that capability to building-attached solar products. The company’s solutions address the weight and installation constraints of conventional glass-based solar modules, which require structural reinforcement on aging industrial buildings and cannot conform to the curved surfaces and design requirements of automotive applications.

Solarstic is developing two core product lines: lightweight BAPV modules for aging factories and low-load roofs, and VIPV components that integrate solar cells directly into vehicle exterior parts. The company is currently conducting four joint development projects with domestic automotive manufacturers and related companies, and has been selected for a government R&D program focused on lightweight vehicle solar module development.

The company plans to use the new capital to complete KS certification for its building solar products and launch commercial sales, while establishing a factory to internalize core VIPV manufacturing processes. Solarstic is targeting KS certification in the second half of 2026 and has been conducting proof-of-concept trials with large industrial companies to validate installation feasibility, power generation performance and field applicability in actual industrial facilities.

The lightweight design reduces structural load and installation complexity, enabling solar deployment on aging industrial sites where conventional glass modules could not be installed. Solarstic intends to begin full commercial sales after KS certification and establish a foothold in the previously underserved aging factory rooftop market.

In vehicle-integrated solar, Solarstic is advancing materials, packaging structures, forming processes and on-vehicle integration technology. The company’s ability to embed solar cells in curved automotive exterior parts while preserving vehicle design was recognized with a CES 2026 Innovation Award Honoree designation in the Vehicle Tech & Advanced Mobility category. Solarstic plans to internalize core VIPV processes to establish automotive-grade quality control systems and convert its current joint development projects into future mass-production programs.

“Solarstic has differentiated technology that enables solar cell integration into vehicle exterior components while preserving the vehicle’s curvature and design,” said Jonghyun Lee, managing director at Stonebridge Ventures, who led the investment. “We rated the technology platform highly for its ability to expand beyond passenger and commercial vehicles into personal mobility vehicles, robotics and autonomous mobile platforms.”

An IBK Bank credit officer said, “Solarstic is opening a new market targeting aging industrial facilities where conventional solar modules were difficult to apply, while also securing a growth foundation in vehicle-integrated photovoltaics through joint development with automotive companies. We viewed positively the business structure that combines the market potential of lightweight building solar with the mid- to long-term growth opportunity of vehicle-integrated solar.”

“This investment marks a turning point as Solarstic moves beyond technology validation and commercialization preparation to full product launch and mass-production infrastructure,” said Sungkeun Park, CEO of Solarstic. “We will successfully bring our lightweight building solar product to market to generate new revenue, and establish a factory to internalize core vehicle solar processes, connecting our current joint development achievements to mass-production projects with automotive manufacturers.”
